Model transfer: uniform draws in [0,1] have densities, so the finitely many proper algebraic bad sets and proper conditional hyperplanes have probability zero. Exceptional dimensions, noninvertibility and invalid blocks can be guarded and return failure within the same polynomial budget. This verifies the weaker success probability 2/3 without claiming a finite-bit-randomness or conditioning theorem.

Avoided an undefined safe-UCQ predicate by using a semantic statement, approved by the parent: every Q either has an equivalent finite UCQ U with weighted PQE(U) in FP, or UR(Q) is #P-hard. Weighted PQE is fully defined with binary rational input and exact rational output. The public card identifies this as a semantic formulation, not as the source's literal wording.

Equivalence audit: let S(Q) mean equivalence to a syntactically safe UCQ in the Dalvi–Suciu sense, T(Q) mean equivalence to a finite UCQ U with PQE(U) in FP, and H(Q) mean Cook #P-hardness of UR(Q). The 2012 author manuscript Definition 4.14 (PDF p. 31) and Theorem 4.21 (PDF p. 33), also restated in PODS 2024 Proposition 3.1 (p. 105:6), give S(Q) => T(Q), and give #P-hardness of weighted PQE(U) for every unsafe U. Also S(Q) unconditionally implies UR(Q) in FP by setting all weights to one half. Thus the source conjecture's substantive assertion forall Q, not S(Q) => H(Q) implies forall Q, T(Q) or H(Q). Conversely assume the semantic assertion and take Q with not S(Q). If H(Q), the source conclusion holds. Otherwise T(Q) supplies a UCQ U equivalent to Q with PQE(U) in FP. U cannot be safe, because that would imply S(Q). The weighted dichotomy makes PQE(U) #P-hard. Composing its Cook reductions with the assumed FP algorithm places every #P function in FP. Consequently every total oracle function UR(Q), even an uncomputable one, is #P-hard: compute the desired #P function directly in polynomial time and make no oracle calls. Hence H(Q) also follows in this branch. This proves equivalence of the universal propositions without assuming FP != #P. It does not assert that syntactic safety and PQE tractability are unconditionally equivalent for each individual UCQ.

The source uses polynomial-time Turing/Cook reductions, not parsimonious or many-one reductions. A hard oracle is not required to be computable or in #P. Algorithms, exponents and reductions may depend on the fixed query; no procedure classifying arbitrary query descriptions is demanded.

Quantifier recovery: CCC 2018 p. 13:2 footnote 3 explicitly points to subexponential versus quasipolynomial time depending on hardness. Its referenced KI 2004 Theorem 7.7, visually checked on pp. 36–37, states s_p(m) in m^{omega(1)} and time 2^{n^epsilon} for every epsilon > 0; the stronger 2^{m^{Omega(1)}} hardness gives quasipolynomial time. Thus the proposed formula analogue uses almost-everywhere superpolynomial growth, not merely an infinitely-often failure of membership in a polynomial-size class. This is an explicit recovery of the cited tradeoff, not a claim that the informal 2018 sentence itself writes all these quantifiers.

Explicitness follows CCC 2018 Definition 10 (p. 13:8), confirmed by journal 2019 Definition 4.7 (p. 12): all coefficient bit lengths are polynomial, and all 2^m coefficients are listed in 2^{O(m)} time. Do not replace this with the stronger per-coefficient polynomial-time condition suggested by an informal journal introduction footnote. Restricting to Q follows the paper's setup; no extension to every field is demanded. Multilinearity applies to the hypothetical hard polynomial family only, not to the circuits that are lower-bounded or the PIT inputs.

Algebraic hardness size counts wires and permits arbitrary rational constants without charging their bit lengths, matching the source's circuit convention. Binary fan-in is a harmless normalization: each unbounded-fan-in formula gate can be replaced by a binary tree with only linear size change. Rational signs can be represented by constants. There is no division or compressed power operation. PIT is a conventional white-box decision problem on the full finite formula description; its bit cost includes constants. Its bit length and reasonable alternative prefix encodings are polynomially related, which leaves membership in the intersection over all epsilon > 0 of DTIME(2^{N^epsilon}) invariant.

The source's displayed bounded-depth runtime is expressed in variables, size and degree. For an explicitly supplied formula, degree and number of distinct variables are at most linear in its tree size, while all input coefficient bits are part of N. The proposed total-bit-length SUBEXP formulation is the ordinary decision-language version of the selected nontrivial runtime regime. It does not demand subexponential complexity independently of arbitrarily large input coefficient encodings or a polynomial-time algorithm. Each epsilon may have a different uniform deterministic machine; no input-length advice, oracle or random coins are allowed.

The existence implication deliberately does not add an effective uniform compiler accepting the generator of any hard family or a proof of its lower bound. The mathematical family is uniform through its coefficient-list algorithm; its lower bound applies to nonuniform formulas. A positive proof is conditional on H and need not construct an unconditional superpolynomial lower bound. A negative proof must establish H and failure of the full D, not merely failure of a particular generator construction.

The saved 'vice-versa' cannot automatically be read as D iff exactly H. KI 2004 Theorem 4.9, visually inspected on p. 25, excludes simultaneous NEXP subset P/poly, polynomial-size division-free integer formulas for permanent, and infinitely-often nondeterministic SUBEXP AFIT. It gives a Boolean-or-arithmetic disjunction, not H alone. Black-box hitting sets give algebraic hardness by a different theorem; a general white-box tester need not output a hitting set. The 2019 survey distinguishes these issues in Sections 3.1–3.2, PDF pp. 7–9. The forward selection preserves a genuine explicitly sourced branch without silently asserting a stronger equivalence.

Negation audit: the target is forall epsilon exists c not Fast(c,epsilon), so its full negation is exists epsilon forall c Fast(c,epsilon). Each c may have its own finite algorithm, word-size constant and runtime constant, while the same positive saving epsilon must work for every c. Merely giving different positive savings epsilon_c tending to zero with c does not refute this formulation. The card does not strengthen the negation by requiring a compiler that takes c as input and produces algorithms.

The directed model is explicit in Fischer footnote 1; original APSP permits directed graphs. The signed weights and no-negative-cycle promise are preserved from 2018 rather than silently changed to nonnegative or unit weights. Fischer footnote 2 states the equivalence of its nonnegative convention to signed weights via a potential reweighting and a sufficiently fast single-source computation. Such normalization may enlarge the polynomial weight exponent, which is allowed by the chosen quantifiers. No equivalence to the fixed-small-weight Strong APSP hypothesis is assumed.

Definitions include a dense explicit matrix, at most one directed edge per ordered pair, possible self-loops, missing-edge flags, zero-weight ties/cycles, unreachable pairs, empty paths, all n^2 exact outputs, and the lack of any requirement to detect a violated negative-cycle promise. Distances of reachable distinct vertices have a simple-path witness with at most n-1 edges, so they fit in O(log n) bits for fixed c. They are not real-valued inputs or approximate outputs. The 1/100 numerical benchmark rule does not change the computational problem inside this yes/no hypothesis.

The finite-program word-RAM convention is a concrete editorial completion of the source's standard logarithmic-word RAM. Word-size factors may depend on fixed c and the algorithm, keeping every word O(log n) bits and permitting all weights and addresses in O(1) words. The explicit instruction set has only conventional word operations; multiword arithmetic, preprocessing, generated tables, random bits and output are charged. It supplies no unbounded-precision real primitive, arbitrary-real advice, nonuniform lookup table or cryptographic/quantum oracle. Using fair words rather than fair bits or simulating word multiplication/division with simpler bit operations changes costs by at most polylogarithmic factors; with a possible smaller epsilon, this preserves whether a fixed truly subcubic saving exists.

Probability/time normalization: Fischer Section 2.5 (printed p. 15/PDF p. 17) allows randomized algorithms succeeding with probability 1-n^{-d} for arbitrarily large constant d. The draft chooses joint matrix success 2/3 and a worst-case bound for every coin sequence. Repeating independently and taking a coordinatewise majority increases whole-matrix success: whenever a majority of complete runs are correct, every coordinate majority is correct. O(log n) repetitions give high probability, adding O(n^2 log n) output-comparison cost and preserving truly subcubic existence after shrinking epsilon. Conversely high probability implies constant success, after harmless treatment of finitely many sizes. These equivalences concern the existence of some positive saving, not equality of one fixed epsilon predicate.

Expected-time variants also do not change the full no-truly-subcubic hypothesis under conventional bounded error: first amplify success to at least 5/6 by a constant number of repetitions, then abort after a sufficiently large constant multiple of the worst-case-over-input expected runtime. Markov's inequality bounds abort probability by at most 1/6, giving joint success at least 2/3 and a worst-case runtime bound. Conversely a worst-case bound implies the same expected bound. The draft itself fixes worst-case time explicitly; it does not confuse average input distributions with per-input randomization. This normalization is an audit explanation, not a proposed APSP solution technique.

The source does not prescribe machine instructions, numeric bit encodings, a random-tape distribution or how the matroid is accessed at the bit level. The exact-real model counts both oracle calls and all intervening work, so it does not silently weaken polynomial time to polynomial query count with unlimited computation. Because the ratio is a supremum, arbitrarily close guarantees may use distinct finite programs and polynomial degrees; no algorithm attaining the endpoint is demanded.

Read the actual CCC2015 publisher PDF, especially Section 2 printed pp. 436–437/PDF4–5, Introduction pp. 434–435, Corollary 4.1 printed p. 441/PDF9, and Section 7 printed p. 446/PDF14. Problem 2 asks about every unsatisfiable CNF in linear total space; n is the number of variables. The input CNF can have arbitrarily many clauses, including exponentially many in n. Neither proof length nor effective proof search is part of the target.

The final source permits a single inference to form a positive-integer combination of arbitrarily many simultaneously stored premises. Footnote 2 explicitly warns that a binary-addition/unary-multiplication presentation may change other complexity measures even though inequality space agrees. The draft therefore retains the source's arbitrary-fan-in rule instead of asserting an unproved constant-factor total-space equivalence between the two presentations. Repeating a premise in a combination is absorbed in its positive multiplier and needs no duplicate set entry.

Section 2 defines total space using all nonzero coefficient binary lengths and the constant term, ignoring signs. Footnote 3 deliberately ignores variable names; charging binary indices may add a logarithmic factor. The draft does not identify this measure with full machine bit space. Taking zero to occupy one binary digit makes the RHS-zero case explicit; it is the usual encoding completion and has no asymptotic effect. Coefficients are canonically collected and constants moved right before charging; no multiplication or gcd reduction is a free normalization.

The proof model uses finite sets of inequalities. A new conclusion is added to the current set while its premises remain present, and erasure is a separate move. Input axioms can be downloaded repeatedly. Fixed original variables, syntactic integer rules, and no extension or semantic inference are specified. The target is proof existence, so no probabilistic computation model or polynomial verification/search budget is imposed. The n+1 convention and zero-variable formulas are an explicit asymptotic edge convention.

The final proceedings give O(n^2) total space, not O(n), in Corollary 4.1 on printed p. 441. The older author-hosted CP_constant_space.pdf has the title date 29 October 2014; its Corollary 6 printed p. 10 says O(n), but its introduction printed p. 3 says O(n^2), and the final proceedings correct the corollary to O(n^2). Read together these are an internal typo in the old draft, not a later resolution. Search-engine freshness metadata for that static PDF must not be read as a 2025 result.

Coefficient audit: sign query zero returns 1 exactly for negative integers; q>=1 returns magnitude bit q-1. Valid q<=d^B covers all bits under |a|<2^(d^B). The coefficient bound is polynomial in degree, while the per-bit running time is polynomial in log degree. For d>=2 any fixed polynomial bound with constant factor can be absorbed by increasing B. Circuit audit: arbitrary complex labels may be noncomputable as bit strings and are free scalars; this intentionally retains the strong source model. Randomized-model inference checked separately: suppose an always-feasible polynomial-time randomized algorithm has expected ratio r<75/74. Choose a fixed reduction gap with no-instance OPT at least bT and yes-instance OPT at most T, with r<b<75/74. On yes instances, Markov gives probability at least1-r/b of output cost<bT; on no instances no tour passes that test. Constant repetition therefore gives a one-sided randomized decision procedure for the NP-hard gap problem. Thus such an algorithm implies NP=RP; assuming NP!=RP excludes all r<75/74, and hence lower-bounds the infimum. The public card labels this as an editorial consequence rather than attributing the exact randomized statement to the paper. P!=NP alone was deliberately not claimed to exclude randomized expected-cost algorithms.

The following paragraph explicitly warns that its failure need not give a fixed-saving algorithm for unrestricted-width CNF-SAT. Preserve the per-width existential algorithm quantifier; do not add one effective algorithm generator for all k.

Polynomial input-factor normalization is substantive and sourced, rather than permitting a vacuous input-reading lower bound on arbitrarily padded formulas. For a fixed width k, removing repeated literals, tautological clauses and duplicate clauses yields at most sum_{j=0}^k 2^j binomial(n,j) distinct non-tautological clauses. The resulting length is polynomial in n for fixed k. Preprocessing arbitrary explicit input costs poly(L); the polynomial length factors on reduced instances can be absorbed by any fixed smaller exponent saving. Thus the full every-epsilon assertion uses the customary polynomial-input-factor normalization without a hidden linear-clause promise. The audit does not assert pointwise equality of exact runtime bounds at a fixed epsilon.

The chosen bounded-error constant is directly supported by Cygan et al. Definition 2.1. The statement permits both false positives and false negatives. For this satisfiability hypothesis the conventional one-sided and two-sided exclusion formulations can also be related with polynomial overhead: amplify a decider to inverse-polynomial error, make at most n adaptive restricted-formula queries to recover a candidate assignment, then verify it. Width does not increase and the number of actual variables does not increase; verification eliminates false positives. This explanatory normalization remains in the audit, not as a public solution hint.

Worst-case time over all fair-coin runs is the BPTIME convention. An expected-time bounded-error speedup with a uniform bound on each input can be amplified by constant repetitions and truncated at a constant multiple of its expected-time bound; the added error can be kept below 1/3. If necessary, choose a smaller rational exponent saving to make the cutoff explicit. Conversely worst-case bounds imply expected bounds. This justifies treating the overall hypothesis as robust to the usual expected-time convention after changing constants or slightly shrinking the saving, not equating every individual machine guarantee. No conversion from arbitrary real/quantum randomness is asserted.

The negation is some one positive epsilon_0 followed by every fixed width and then an algorithm and constants for that width. The program need not be the same for different widths, but is finite and uniform in input size for each width. A particular small-width speedup, a width-dependent saving tending to zero, or a mere sparse/random/unique-input result cannot refute this quantified statement. Positive lower-bound proofs must also address two-sided randomized machines. No conjectural premise is built into either answer.

Root and independent reviewer checked Rothvoss1311.2369v4 PDF3: PM_n is a face of MATCH_n, obtained by sum_e x_e=n/2. Machine-invariance audit: write A_U for the selected forall-c/exists-d proposition with a fixed U. Suppose A_U holds and V is another member of the stated class. Fix V’s sampler exponent c. Any V-simple description has m < n^c because |p| + log_2 m < c log_2 n. Simulating its program on U adds a fixed b_1 to program length and costs at most a fixed polynomial in m+n^c. Choose an integer C > c sufficiently large so that, for all sufficiently large n, every such sampler becomes U-simple at budgets n^C and C log_2 n. Apply A_U at C to get D > C. The converse U-to-V simulation, now on deterministic descriptions with empty other inputs, gives for a sufficiently large integer d > c the inequality C_V^(n^d)(x) <= C_U^(n^D)(x) + b_2 whenever the latter is finite, for all sufficiently large n. Both simulation constants are independent of c,D,n and x once U,V are fixed.

Continuing that audit, each V-simple distribution on a U-witness x satisfies mu(x) <= n^(-C) 2^(-C_U^(n^D)(x)) <= 2^(b_2) n^(-C) 2^(-C_V^(n^d)(x)) <= n^(-c) 2^(-C_V^(n^d)(x)) after increasing the length threshold. If the U complexity is infinite, its zero exponential already forces mu(x)=0; if it is finite, the simulated V description exists. Removing finitely many lengths preserves infinitely many witnesses. Therefore A_U implies A_V, and symmetry gives equivalence. Since ordinary universal simulation supplies at least one machine in the class, forall U is equivalent to fixing any one of these universal machines. This is a model-equivalence check, not a proposed approach to solving A.

The source leaves log 0 undefined. The selected convention requires m >= 1 and permits a dummy unused fair bit, so deterministic samplers remain possible. Time is the maximum of U execution times after the random string is supplied, as in the source. Charging m additional coin-preparation steps would change sampler costs only by a polynomial absorbed by the same exponent transfer, because the length budget implies m < n^c. Description length is the real value |p|+log_2 m, not a guessed binary pair encoding. Samplers must halt and output an n-bit string on every coin string; finite support, dyadic probabilities and exact equality are explicit.

Hypotheses are all rational distributions on strings of one fixed length. Simplicity is existential exact sampling, so realized hypotheses are dyadic; no efficient point-probability evaluator is demanded. The source explicitly calls out that different simplicity requirement separately for Theorem 18. Restricting to efficiently evaluable distributions, uniform distributions on sets or a particular sampler family would weaken the positive impossibility requirement and is not the selected target.

Square-basis model bridge, kept in audit rather than public hints: the published transfer can output a full-column-rank rectangular integer matrix B. It has a deterministic polynomial-time conversion to a square integer basis without changing a fixed-radius decision. Compute an integer basis C for the rational orthogonal complement of B by exact Gaussian elimination and clearing denominators. Set M=ceil(b)+1, which is strictly greater than sqrt(b) for every b>0. Then D=[B,MC] is square and nonsingular; every nonzero C component has squared norm at least M^2 because C has integer entries and independent columns, and is orthogonal to B.
